NEW JERSEY PARCC 2016 SGP ANALYSES

Damian W Betebenner
National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment
Dover, NH March 4th, 2016

BACKGROUND

• 2016 SGP analyses of New Jersey PARCC data were
conducted in December 2015/January 2016

• Analyses were conducted using PARCC theta values (instead
of scaled scores) and scale scores for NJASK as priors to avoid
any potential issues with ceiling/ oor effects.

• Of the 4 PARCC states we work with on SGP analyses, 3
are using theta values.

• Results from SGP analyses (only ELA and Mathematics) are
used, in part, for educator evaluation.

RESULTS: DATA ANALYSIS
• EOGTs are analyzed based upon same content area and
consecutive grades.

• EOCTs are analyzed based upon same/similar content area
(e.g., Mathematics to Algebra I) but not necessarily consecutive
grades:
• 2013 Math, Grade 8 to 2015 Algebra I; 2014 Math, Grade 7 to 2015 Algebra 1; 2014 Math, Grade 8 to 2015
Algebra 1

• 2013 Math, Grade 8 to 2015 Algebra II;

• 2013 Math, Grade 8 to 2015 Geometry: 2014 Math, Grade 8 to 2015 Geometry

RESULTS: SGP PROPERTIES

• SGPs are uncorrelated with prior achievement at the student
level (i.e., a conditional probability)

• SGPs are correlated with current achievement. I.e., higher
growth is associated with higher achievement and vice-versa.

• SGPs for students are uncorrelated from year to year.

“It is a common misconception
that to measure student growth
in education, the subject matter
and grades over which growth is
examined must be on the same
scale—referred to as a vertical
scale. Not only is a vertical scale
not necessary, but its existence
obscures fundamental concepts
necessary to understand growth.”

A Math Story Problem
Properties that don’t hold with simple examples will not hold in
complicated situations. This simple example illustrates how minimally
helpful a scale is to understanding change.

• A vertical scale allows one to answer a
very narrow question: Who changed
more?
• Remarkable & improvement need not be
synonymous with change.
• This example (ratio scale, no
measurement error) illustrates that a
vertical scale is of little help in answering
substantive questions.

“One Year’s Growth”
If “one year’s growth” is to be useful as a value
that makes points on the score scale
more meaningful, it would be useful to know if
the empirical average value of “one
year’s growth” is very different for students at
different levels of the score scale or
from different demographic backgrounds.
Because values for “one year’s growth”
are not currently available, the answers to these
questions are unknown.
David Thissen
